summary: Describes why it is useful to move context between nodes in an IP access network when a mobile host changes subnets. Services such as AAA, header compression and QoS would otherwise need to be set up again from scratch after each move.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3374 explains the problem of context transfer. When a laptop or phone moves to a different part of the network, the services it had, such as being logged in, compressed headers and reserved quality of service, have to be set up again. The memo argues for moving that information from the old router to the new one instead, and sets out what that costs and where it does not help.

subtitle: Why a moving host should be able to carry its network state with it instead of rebuilding it from scratch

tldr.problem: When a mobile host changes subnet, the routers on the new path must offer the same treatment to its packets as the old path did, and services such as authentication, header compression and quality of service usually have to be negotiated again from the start.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of making the host redo every exchange, the memo proposes moving the state those services built, called context, from the old router to the new one, so the services can be put back in place quickly.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a problem statement for the Seamoby working group rather than a protocol. It sets out the two reasons for doing this, the four cases where it will not help, and the security price, which is that a compromise of one router now exposes everything the transferred context covered.

today: RFC 3374 is an Informational memo from September 2002 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a problem statement addressed to the Seamoby working group, asking for an investigation and a protocol rather than defining one, and it points at the mobile IP and header compression work of the time for the technical detail.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
In networks where hosts are mobile, the routing path through the network must often be changed in order to deliver the host's IP traffic to the new point of access. Changing the basic routing path is the job of an IP mobility protocol, such as Mobile IPv4 or Mobile IPv6. But the success of real time services such as VoIP telephony and video in a mobile environment depends heavily on minimising the impact of this traffic redirection. In the process of establishing the new routing path, the nodes along the new path must be prepared to provide similar routing treatment to the IP packets as was provided along the old routing path.

The routing treatment of IP packets within a network may be regulated by a collection of context transfer-candidate services that influence how packets for the host are treated. For example, whether a particular host has the right to obtain any routing at all out of the local subnet may depend on whether the host negotiated a successful AAA exchange with a network access server at some point in the past. Establishing these services initially results in a certain amount of related state within the network and requires a perhaps considerable amount of time for the protocol exchanges. If the host is required to re-establish those services by the same process it uses to initially establish them, delay-sensitive real time traffic may be seriously impacted.

An alternative is to transfer enough information on the context transfer-candidate service state, or context, to the new subnet so that the services can be re-established quickly, rather than require the mobile host to establish them from scratch. The transfer of service context may be advantageous in minimising the impact of host mobility on AAA, header compression, QoS, policy, and possibly sub-IP protocols and services such as PPP. Context transfer at a minimum can be used to replicate the configuration information needed to establish the respective protocols and services, and it may also provide the capability to replicate state information, allowing stateful protocols and services at the new node to be activated along the new path with less delay and less signalling overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving host means new routers must treat its traffic the same way the old ones did. The usual answer is to make the host sign in again and renegotiate everything, which is slow. The proposal is to send the old router's state to the new router instead.

sections.title: What the Problem Covers
sections.content:
Context is the information on the current state of a service required to re-establish the service on a new subnet without having to perform the entire protocol exchange with the mobile host from scratch. Context transfer is the movement of context from one router or other network entity to another as a means of re-establishing specific services on a new subnet or collection of subnets. A context transfer candidate service is a service that is a candidate for context transfer; in this document, only services that are concerned with the forwarding treatment of packets, such as QoS and security, or involve granting or denying the mobile host access to the network, such as AAA, are considered to be context transfer-candidate services.

The context transfer problem examined in the memo is restricted to re-establishing services for a mobile host that are related to the forwarding treatment of the mobile host's packets, or to network access for the mobile host. It is not concerned with actually re-establishing routing information: routing changes due to mobility are the domain of the IP mobility protocol. Transfer of context related to application-level services, such as those associated with the mobile host's HTTP proxy, is also not considered, although a generic context transfer protocol for transferring the context of services related to forwarding treatment or network access may also function for application-level services as well.

An important consideration in whether a service is a candidate for context transfer is whether it is possible to obtain a correct context transfer for the service in a given implementation and deployment, that is, one which will result in the same context at the new access router as would have resulted had the mobile host undergone a protocol exchange with the access router from scratch. For some services, the circumstances under which context transfer may result in correctness may be very limited.
sections.plainLanguage: Only services that decide how packets are treated or whether the host may have network access are in scope. Routing itself is left to the mobility protocol, and application-level services are not covered.

sections.title: Why Context Transfer Is Wanted
sections.content:
There are two basic motivations for context transfer. The primary motivation is the need to quickly re-establish context transfer-candidate services without requiring the mobile host to explicitly perform all protocol flows for those services from scratch. An additional motivation is to provide an interoperable solution that works for any Layer 2 radio access technology.

For AAA, one of the more compelling applications is facilitating re-authentication of the mobile host and re-establishment of its authorisation for network access in a new subnet, by transferring the AAA context from the mobile host's previous AAA server to another. This would allow the host to continue access in the new subnet without having to redo an AAA exchange with the new subnet's AAA server. Naturally, a security association between the AAA servers is necessary so that the mobile host's sensitive authentication information can be transferred securely. Without context transfer there are two ways that can currently be used for AAA: Layer 2 mechanisms, such as EAP in PPP or 802.1x, can be used to redo the initial protocol exchange, or possibly to update it, and currently there is no general Layer 3 mechanism for conducting an AAA exchange between a host and an AAA server in the network; or, if the mobile host is using Mobile IPv4 but not Mobile IPv6, the host can use the AAA registration keys extension for Mobile IPv4 to establish a security association with the new Foreign Agent. That second option is piggybacked on the Mobile IPv4 signalling, so the performance is less likely to be an issue, but it is not a general solution, and the performance of the first is likely to be considerably less than is necessary for maintaining good real time stream performance.

For header compression, establishing compression generally requires from 1 to 4 exchanges between the last hop router and the mobile host with full or partially compressed headers before full compression is available. During this period the host experiences an effective reduction in the application-available bandwidth equal to the uncompressed header information sent over the air. Context transfer helps here by allowing the network entity performing header compression, usually the last hop router, to transfer the header compression context to the new router. The timing must be arranged so that the header context is transferred from the old router as soon as the host is no longer receiving packets through it, and installed on the new router before any packets are delivered to or forwarded from the host.

For QoS, significant protocol exchanges between the mobile host and routers may be required to establish the initial treatment for the host's packets, and preliminary studies for existing approaches have indicated that the flows necessary to re-establish QoS in a new subnet from scratch can be very time consuming for Mobile IP. A method of transferring the host's QoS context from the old network to the new could facilitate faster re-establishment. However, for QoS mechanisms that are end-to-end, transferring context at the last hop router may be insufficient, since some number of additional routers in the path between the host and the corresponding node may also need to be involved.

On interoperability, different Layer 2 radio protocols may define their own solutions for context transfer, and there are ongoing efforts within 3GPP and IEEE to define such solutions, primarily designed to transfer Layer 2-related context over a wired IP network between two radio access networks or two radio access points. These designs can include extensibility features that would allow Layer 3 context to be transferred. If Layer 2 protocols were widely adopted as an optimisation for Layer 3 context transfer, seamless mobility of a host that has Layer 2 interfaces supporting multiple radio protocols would be difficult to achieve, because a gateway or translator between the Layer 2 protocols would be required, or the host would have to perform a full re-initialisation of its context transfer-candidate services on the new radio network if no translator were available.
sections.plainLanguage: Two reasons: it saves time when the host signs in again, negotiates compression or asks for a quality level, and one solution at the IP layer works whatever radio technology the network uses underneath.

sections.title: Where Context Transfer Does Not Help
sections.content:
Context transfer may not always be the best solution for re-establishing context transfer-candidate services on a new subnet, and there are four limitations on when it may be useful.

Router compatibility: context transfer between two routers is possible only if the receiving router supports the same context transfer-candidate services as the sending router. This does not mean that the two nodes are identical in their implementation, nor does it imply that they must have identical capabilities. A router that cannot make use of received context should refuse the transfer. This results in a situation no different than a mobile host handover without context transfer, and should not be considered an error or failure situation.

Requirement to re-initialise the service from scratch: the primary motivation for context transfer assumes that quickly re-establishing the same level of service on the new subnet is desirable. There may be situations where either the device or the access network would prefer to re-establish or re-negotiate the level of service, for example if the host crosses administrative domains where the operational policies change, in which case negotiation of a different level of service may be required.

Suitability for the particular service: context transfer assumes that it is faster to establish the service by context transfer rather than from scratch. This may not be true for certain types of service, for example multicast, push information services.

Layer 2 solutions better: context transfer is an enhancement to improve upon the performance of a handover for Layer 3 context transfer-candidate services. Many networks provide support for handover at Layer 2, within and between subnets, so Layer 3 context transfer may not provide a significant improvement over Layer 2 solutions, even for Layer 3 context, if the handover is occurring between two subnets supporting the same Layer 2 radio access technology.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not help when the new router cannot use what it is sent, when the host or the network would rather renegotiate the service from scratch, when the service is one that is quicker to set up afresh, or when the radio layer already handles the handover well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any context transfer standard must provide a mechanism for adequately securing the context transfer process, and a recommendation to deploy security, as is typically the case for Internet standards. Three general considerations apply. Information privacy: the context may contain information which the end user or network operator would prefer to keep hidden from unauthorised viewers. Transfer legitimacy: a false or purposely corrupted context transfer could have a severe impact upon the operation of the receiving router, and therefore could potentially affect the operation of the access network itself, with the potential threats including denial of service and theft of service attacks. Security preservation: part of the context transfer may include information pertinent to a security association established between the mobile host and another entity on the network, and for that security association to be preserved during handover, the transfer of the security context must include the appropriate security measures.

It is expected that the measures used to secure the transport of information between peers, for example IPsec, in an IP network should be sufficient for context transfer. However, given the above considerations, there may be reason to provide for additional security measures beyond the available IETF solutions.

Since context transfer requires a trust relationship between network entities, the compromise of only one of the network entities that transfer context may be sufficient to reduce the security of the whole system, if for example the context transferred includes encryption keying material. When the host moves from the compromised network entity to an uncompromised network entity in the presence of context transfer, the compromised context may be used to decrypt the communication channel. When context transfer is not used, a compromise of only one network entity only gives access to what that network entity can see, and when the mobile host moves to an uncompromised network entity, security can be re-established at the new entity. However, to the extent that context transfer happens primarily between routers, the security of context transfer will depend on the security of the routers. Any compromise of security on a router that affects context transfer may also lead to other, equally serious disruptions in network traffic. The context transfer investigation must identify any novel security measures required for context transfer that exceed the capabilities of the existing or emerging IETF solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving state between routers means the two routers must trust each other. That trust cuts both ways: if one router is broken into, the attacker inherits everything the transferred state covered, and the host's protection can be broken rather than rebuilt.

sections.title: What the Memo Asks For
sections.content:
The memo recommends two steps for the Seamoby working group: an investigation into candidate router-related services for context, with an analysis of the transfer requirements for each candidate, and the development of a framework and protocols that will support the transfer of context between the routing nodes of an IP network. The context transfer solution must inter-work with existing and emerging IP protocols, in particular those protocols supporting mobility in an IP network.

The purpose of context transfer is to sustain the context transfer-candidate services being provided to a mobile host's traffic during handover. It is essentially an enhancement to IP mobility that ultimately must result in an improvement in handover performance. A context transfer solution must provide performance that is equal to or better than re-initialising the context transfer-candidate service between the mobile host and the network from scratch. Otherwise, context transfer is of no benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo asks the working group to work out which services are worth moving state for, and then to build a framework and protocol for moving it, in a way that works with the mobility protocols already in use. If the result is not faster than starting again, there is no point.
